questions: J
Is malaria caused by a virus or by bacteria?
Neither. It is caused by a single-celled parasite called Plasmodium. That is also why a vaccine was so difficult to make (WHO, 2025a).
J
Why does only the female mosquito spread malaria?
Only female Anopheles mosquitoes bite people: they need blood to produce their eggs. Males feed on plant juices.
J
Can I get malaria from another person?
Not like a cold. It needs a mosquito. In rare cases it can pass through blood, for example a transfusion, or from a mother to her baby.
M
Why is the disease called malaria?
From the Italian mal aria, "bad air". People thought the air of the swamps caused it. Today we know it is the mosquito that lives near the swamps (Cox, 2010).
M
Who discovered the parasite?
Alphonse Laveran, a French army doctor, in Algeria in 1880. Ronald Ross then showed the mosquito link in 1897, and Grassi's team proved it was Anopheles in 1898.
M
Why did the 1934–35 epidemic in Ceylon start?
A drought dried the rivers into small pools: perfect places for mosquito larvae. About 80,000 people died (Gill, 1935).
R
Why is Africa hit hardest?
It has the most dangerous parasite, P. falciparum, very efficient mosquitoes, a warm climate, and many people far from clinics. That is why it has 94% of cases (WHO, 2025b).
R
Is there malaria in Uzbekistan today?
No local transmission: the last local cases were in 2010 and WHO certified us malaria-free in 2018. Travellers can still bring cases from abroad, so testing continues (WHO, 2018).
R
If we have the tools, why are cases rising?
The population grows, funding is only 42% of what is needed, and there is drug resistance, floods and conflict, for example in Ethiopia and Yemen (WHO, 2025b).
A
How effective is the vaccine?
R21 reduced cases by 75% in seasonal areas in the first year, and in the pilot child deaths fell by 13%. It is not 100%, so nets are still needed (WHO, 2023b; 2025b).
A
What is ACT?
Artemisinin-based combination therapy: artemisinin plus a second medicine. Two medicines together make it harder for the parasite to become resistant (WHO, 2025a).
A
What should a traveller do?
See a doctor before the trip, take preventive tablets, use repellent and a net. If fever starts after returning, test immediately and say where you travelled.
